title: Oil Prices Near $100 as Iran War Disrupts Global Energy Supplies
author: Michael Chen
image: /images/news/Oil and Gas Prices Surge as Iran War Raises Global Energy Supply Fears.webp
excerpt: Oil and gas prices are surging as the Iran war disrupts shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, threatens supply and raises global inflation risks.
content: Oil and gas markets are once again under intense pressure as renewed fighting involving the United States and Iran raises fears that disruptions around the Middle East could turn into a much larger global energy supply shock. Brent crude moved toward the $100-a-barrel threshold on Monday, September 7, after rising 1.2% to $97.47 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate gained to $92.26. The latest rally followed renewed attacks involving tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for international energy shipments. Markets are increasingly pricing the possibility that the conflict could keep oil and gas supplies constrained for an extended period rather than producing only a short-lived geopolitical premium.

The Strait of Hormuz is at the centre of the latest concern. The waterway connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and is one of the world's most important energy corridors. Iranian forces have restricted traffic through the strait since the conflict began, and the number of commercial vessels moving through the passage has fallen sharply. Reuters reported that an average of only about 10 commodity ships a day had transited the strait during the previous 10 days, the lowest level since May. Iran has also said it plans to announce a new restricted zone in the Persian Gulf and publish revised shipping corridors, raising fresh uncertainty for shipowners, insurers and energy traders.

For oil markets, even the threat of a prolonged shipping disruption can be powerful enough to move prices higher. The Gulf remains a major source of crude exports for global consumers, and an extended reduction in tanker traffic could remove significant volumes from international trade. The International Energy Agency said in its August oil market report that global supply had already fallen sharply below year-earlier levels, with 8.3 million barrels per day of Gulf production still shut in at the time of its analysis. The agency projected global oil supply to decline by 4.3 million barrels per day on average in 2026, while global inventories had fallen by hundreds of millions of barrels since the beginning of the war.

The pressure is particularly severe because the disruption is not limited to crude oil. Refineries across the Middle East and elsewhere are also dealing with logistical constraints, damaged infrastructure and changing economics. Reuters reported on Monday that global refiners are increasingly prioritizing more profitable products such as diesel and gasoline, reducing the amount of fuel oil available for ships and power generation. A global fuel-oil deficit of about 218,000 barrels per day is now forecast for the third quarter, compared with a much smaller shortfall a year earlier. Fuel-oil inventories at major hubs including Singapore, Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp and Fujairah were reported to be around 30% below seasonal norms.

Natural gas is facing a particularly complicated outlook. Unlike crude oil, LNG shipments from the Gulf depend heavily on specific export infrastructure and maritime routes. Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are major LNG suppliers, but the conflict has disrupted cargo movements through the Strait of Hormuz. Some LNG producers and traders have resorted to unusual ship-to-ship transfers outside the strait in an attempt to keep cargoes moving. Reuters reported that three Qatari and UAE LNG cargoes were transferred at sea off Oman and the UAE before continuing toward customers including India and Japan. Asian spot LNG prices had climbed to about $23.20 per million British thermal units, more than double their pre-conflict level.

That has significant consequences for Asia because the region relies heavily on imported LNG for power generation and industrial use. Higher spot prices make it more expensive for utilities and manufacturers to secure additional cargoes when contracted supplies are disrupted. Smaller Asian economies may struggle to compete for limited spot-market cargoes against wealthier buyers, while countries with existing long-term contracts could become more dependent on those agreements. The shift can also encourage traders to redirect LNG cargoes between Europe and Asia depending on which market offers the strongest price, tightening supply in one region when another becomes more lucrative.

Europe faces its own exposure. Gas markets are already sensitive to the loss of Middle Eastern LNG supply, and European benchmark prices have risen sharply during periods of heightened conflict. The IEA has warned that the Middle East war has profoundly changed the natural-gas outlook, with the temporary loss of close to 20% of global LNG supply earlier in the conflict driving prices in Asia and Europe to their highest levels since the 2022-23 energy crisis. Damage to Qatar's LNG infrastructure has also raised concerns about longer-term supply growth, delaying the expected easing that would have come from new liquefaction capacity.

The economic consequences extend well beyond energy companies. Higher oil prices increase transportation and manufacturing costs, while expensive gas affects electricity generation, heating, chemicals and fertilizer production. Shipping is particularly vulnerable because higher bunker-fuel prices raise the cost of moving goods around the world. Reuters said very-low-sulphur fuel-oil prices in Singapore had risen 76% since the beginning of the Iran war, significantly faster than Brent crude, which had gained around 40%. Higher marine fuel costs could therefore add another layer of inflation to already strained global supply chains.

The inflation risk is becoming increasingly important for central banks. A prolonged oil and gas shock can raise headline inflation even when underlying domestic demand is cooling. Europe is already facing renewed monetary-policy pressure as higher energy costs push inflation higher. Reuters reported that the European Central Bank is expected to raise its policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% at its September meeting, partly because energy-related inflation has remained persistent. The possibility of additional tightening could create a difficult trade-off between controlling inflation and protecting economic growth.

For the United States, higher oil prices create a different set of risks. American consumers are already facing elevated gasoline and diesel costs, while businesses that rely heavily on trucking, aviation and logistics face larger operating expenses. US diesel prices recently reached a record high amid the global refined-fuel shortage. The combination of expensive crude and tight refining capacity could therefore feed into consumer prices across transportation, agriculture, construction and retail.

China is another crucial variable for the market. The world's largest oil importer has been forced to adapt to weaker Middle Eastern supply flows. Reuters reported that China's seaborne crude imports averaged about 7.14 million barrels per day in August, roughly 40% below pre-conflict levels. Chinese refiners have responded by reducing some processing activity or paying higher prices for alternative supplies, while imports from Russia have increased. China's ability to secure replacement barrels will be an important indicator of whether the global market can absorb the disruption without an even sharper price rise.

Supply diversification is already becoming a strategic priority. Gulf producers are looking for alternative export routes that can bypass vulnerable maritime chokepoints. The UAE, for example, is developing additional eastern port capacity and investing in pipelines, railways and other trade corridors to reduce its dependence on routes exposed to the conflict. Such investments will not immediately replace the capacity of the Strait of Hormuz, but they demonstrate how governments and energy companies are beginning to reassess infrastructure after months of disruption.

The biggest question now is whether oil prices can move decisively above $100 or retreat if shipping conditions improve. Analysts are already warning that a deeper supply shock could push prices considerably higher. Goldman Sachs said Monday that oil could rise as high as $120 a barrel if attacks on shipping in the Middle East intensify. Such a move would represent a major additional shock for importers and could rapidly amplify inflationary pressures across the global economy.

At the same time, the market has reasons not to assume that prices will rise indefinitely. High energy costs themselves reduce consumption, encourage efficiency and make alternative sources more competitive. Producers outside the conflict zone can also increase output where spare capacity exists, while governments can release strategic reserves or introduce emergency measures. The IEA has already highlighted how demand is being reduced by elevated fuel prices and disrupted economic activity. Its August forecast projected global oil demand to decline by 1.6 million barrels per day in 2026 before returning to growth in the final quarter.

Still, the immediate market signal is clear: the Iran war has transformed a regional security crisis into a global energy-market problem. Oil is approaching $100 a barrel, LNG costs in Asia remain dramatically above pre-war levels, marine fuel markets are tightening and governments are preparing for a potentially prolonged disruption. Every additional attack on shipping or energy infrastructure increases the possibility of a larger supply shock.

For investors, the next phase of the crisis will depend less on individual military headlines and more on whether physical energy flows can continue. Tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, Gulf production, LNG exports from Qatar and the UAE, Russian refinery operations, Chinese crude imports and global inventory levels will all determine how far prices can rise. If disruptions persist, energy may become one of the strongest sources of inflation pressure across the global economy. If shipping gradually normalizes, the sharp geopolitical premium currently embedded in prices could unwind quickly.

Markets will closely monitor tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, further Iranian restrictions on shipping, attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure and the response of Qatar, the UAE and Saudi Arabia. Oil traders will also watch whether Brent breaks decisively above $100 and whether the market begins pricing the $120 scenario warned about by Goldman Sachs. In gas markets, LNG cargo availability in Asia and Europe will be critical, particularly as buyers prepare for the Northern Hemisphere winter.
